title: Through My Clerkships in Beijing
paragraphs: I experienced clerkships in Beijing, China, and spent two months a little different from ordinary student life. In an environment where both language and culture were different, as I attended daily medical care and interacted with local medical students and doctors, there was much bewilderment and many realizations. Unlike clinical clerkships in Japan, there were many scenes in which I was strongly conscious of being a "student from outside," and there were quite a few things that did not go well. Even so, there were experiences and perspectives that could be obtained only there, and after returning home I gradually came to feel their value. In this account, I would like to look back, from my own perspective, on the preparation before departure, what I learned during the clerkships, and fragments of daily life.

The hardest thing was, after all, preparing the documents. I was overwhelmed by the number of required documents, and for someone like me who finds things troublesome, it was honestly quite stressful. In particular, I often did not know what to write for things like the study abroad plan and the statement of motivation. To pass the internal selection, submission of an English score was necessary, and I chose IELTS, but I did not reach the target score the first two times and was quite anxious. When I finally exceeded the standard on the third attempt, right at the submission deadline, and was able to apply, I was truly relieved. Also, because it was a long study abroad of two months, I was very anxious about the timing of the hospital visits and the effect on preparation for the national examination and the graduation examination. But I remember that I steeled myself, thinking "since I'm going, I have to do it," and departed.

This time I was allowed to observe two surgical departments, one month each. Since I could not enter the surgical field, it was basically centered on observing operations, and honestly I got a bit bored in the latter half. Personally, I do not recommend spending the whole period on surgery. But then I do not know what clerkships in internal medicine are like either, which is a dilemma. As for the operations themselves, there were differences from Japan in surgical techniques, speed, and the instruments and drugs used, and it was interesting to observe such points. I also had the chance to hear about differences in the doctors' positions and ways of working, and being able to feel the differences in healthcare systems was a big learning. The supervising doctor in hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery who looked after me in the first month spoke Japanese very fluently and his wife also spoke Japanese, so it was a very easy environment. When I had any trouble I could consult him right away, and it helped me quite a lot mentally.

On site, QR code payment is extremely developed, and for me, who did not have a Chinese resident ID, even small payments in daily life were often a struggle. There were many places where cash could not be used, and I felt the inconvenience every time I ate or shopped. As for food, I had an impression completely different from the Chinese food I was familiar with in Japan. The local dishes varied greatly in taste and quality depending on the price, and I struggled because the food did not suit me. For two months I was even thinking about "how to spend my time without eating Chinese food." Also, for me, who did not understand Chinese at all, the language barrier was big in both daily life and the clerkships. Few local people could speak English, and even in the hospital I could hardly hold a conversation with anyone other than my supervising doctor. In that situation, being able to become friends with a Japanese student of the Peking University medical school was a great support. Without that connection, I think it would have been even harder to get through these two months.

There was a lot that bewildered me on site, but that too was a valuable experience. Not only the clerkship content but also differences in environment and moments of realizing my own immaturity made what I gained not small. This experience may not be useful for anything right away, but I feel that someday, when I happen to remember it, it will become something that supports me.
